title: The elephant's footprint
hookLine: as every footprint fits inside an elephant's, every good teaching fits inside the four truths (MN 28)

lines: A DEER, A JACKAL, A BOAR.
cards: Mud after rain, on a forest track in northern India. A deer has crossed here, and a jackal, and a wild boar, and something small with claws. Their prints crisscross everywhere.

And then, right in the middle, one print so wide you could set every other print inside it with room to spare. An elephant came this way. Year two of the path is the Buddha's own words, and it begins with that footprint.
It isn't the Buddha who points to it, though. It's one of his chief students, standing up before the monks to explain how everything fits together.

teach.b: The student is Sariputta, the monk tradition remembers for his wisdom. The talk is number twenty-eight in the Middle-Length Discourses, and its name means the great simile of the elephant's footprint.

Sariputta tells the monks: just as the footprints of every creature that walks fit inside an elephant's, the biggest of them all, so every good and wholesome teaching fits inside the four noble truths. Then he names them.
The truth of dukkha, the pain and unsatisfactoriness of life. The truth of where it comes from. The truth that it can end.
The truth of the way that leads there.
You met all four in year one. Here's the surprise. Sariputta doesn't wander off into lofty ideas.

He spends most of the talk on the first truth, and he gets very ordinary: your body, made of earth, water, fire and air; the hair, the bones, the breath. He even talks about being insulted and hit, and how to stay steady.
The biggest footprint isn't somewhere far off.

teach.h: THE PRINT RUNS THROUGH A DAY.
teach.b: It runs right through a regular day.

That's the plan for the next three weeks: each truth, one at a time, in the Buddha's own words where the texts give them; then the jobs the Buddha gave each truth; then the chain of causes underneath them.
Whatever you learn later about generosity, kindness, meditation or ethics, this sutta's claim is that it's already inside this one print.

how: Buddhist teachers in different schools present the four noble truths as a frame for the rest of the teaching, and they are often recited in short form at the start of a talk or retreat.

o: the path an elephant clears through a forest
a trail of prints left by a herd of deer
the elephant's print that holds every other print

games.q: match each piece of today's talk.
p: the student who gives the talk
the great simile of the elephant's footprint

s: the Buddha himself gives the elephant's footprint talk in MN 28
it's Sariputta, his student praised for wisdom, who gives it.
after naming the four truths, Sariputta spends the talk on the body and daily life
he works through the first truth with earth, water, fire and air, and even being insulted.
the footprint is a later Zen image
it comes from the Pali Middle-Length Discourses, sutta 28.

games.q: you're one of the monks listening. Sariputta has just said every good teaching fits inside the four truths. where do you expect him to go next?
o: into lofty ideas about the cosmos.
into the first truth, through the body and ordinary trouble.
into a list of other teachers' mistakes.
games.why: he goes straight into the first truth: the body's elements, and even how to stay steady when someone insults or strikes you.

practice: Sit comfortably and walk the four truths, one per breath: there is dukkha; it has a cause; it can end; there is a way.
Go around them slowly, like stepping into four prints in the mud, and if your mind wanders, start again at the first. Nothing to solve, just the outline of the footprint.

wordCard.voice: Hatthipada. The elephant's footprint: Sariputta's image for the four noble truths, the one print large enough to hold every other good teaching.

orig.note: Pali hatthipada: the elephant's footprint, from the sutta's title Mahāhatthipadopama.

carryVoice: Your line: the biggest footprint. Even an ordinary day fits inside the first truth. Year two has begun.

sources.ref: MN 28 (Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, the great simile of the elephant's footprint)
